seoTitle.en: Heroes of the Snowy Alps: the real animals behind Eight Times Up

description.en: A goat-antelope saved by law, snow monkeys that go fishing, and a 'thunder bird' that turns white in winter. Real, checked facts for kids.

intro.en: Every animal in Eight Times Up is real, and they all live in the snowy mountains of central Japan. Here is how they eat, grow and survive the winter.
The book's mountains have no name, so we picked one valley where serows, snow monkeys and rock ptarmigans all live: Kamikochi, in Chubusangaku National Park.

text.en: Chubusangaku National Park was created in 1934 and covers most of the Northern Alps.
Kamikochi sits about 1,500 metres above sea level, and private cars aren't allowed in, to protect it.
The name "Japanese Alps" was given by William Gowland, an English mining engineer, in the 1800s.
Around 140 bird species have been recorded around Kamikochi, including the raichō.
Groundwater-fed streams in Kamikochi stay about 5 °C all winter, which is why snow monkeys can go fishing there.
A mountain valley along the Azusa River in Chubusangaku National Park, home to serows, snow monkeys and, higher up, raichō.

title.en: Not a goat, not a deer

text.en: Its Japanese name, kamoshika, has the word for deer in it, but the serow is really a goat-antelope, a cousin of goats.
A baby is born in May or June and follows its mother for about a year. It may stay in her territory for 2 to 4 years.
Serows have glands under their eyes that make a sweet-sour smell. They rub it on trees to say "this is my patch".
In winter they browse twigs and evergreen leaves poking out of the snow. Older moms can lose about a fifth of their weight by spring.
Serows were hunted almost to extinction by the mid-1900s. Japan made them a Special Natural Monument in 1955, and now there are many again.
Both boys and girls have short horns, 12 to 16 cm long, that keep growing their whole life.
Serows are counted as daytime animals, but a radio-collar study found they're almost as busy at night!

storyVsReal.en: Real serows are great climbers on steep, snowy slopes. But they live alone, not in a herd of big goats racing to Cloud Rock, and Yuki's white star is our artist's idea.

text.en: Japanese macaques live farther north than any other monkey or ape except people. A thick fur coat keeps them warm, because they don't hibernate.
Babies ride on Mom's tummy for the first four weeks, then on her tummy or back until about one year old.
They have six groups of calls. More than half are calm, friendly sounds; one loud holler warns of danger.

In Kamikochi's snowy winters, scientists filmed snow monkeys turning over rocks in warm spring-fed streams to catch fish and water insects. It was the first proof of Japanese macaques eating river fish!
At Shiga Heights, one troop started bathing in warm volcanic hot springs, probably to warm up.
On one island, a young female started washing sweet potatoes in the sea. Soon others in her troop copied her. Monkeys can learn from each other!
In winter, more than 70% of their foraging in Kamikochi is for tree bark and bamboo leaves sticking out of the snow.

storyVsReal.en: Real snow monkeys do play with stones and snow. But the little red roly-poly toy is from Japanese folk tradition, not the forest, and a real macaque has a short stumpy tail.

title.en: Out of the nest on day one

text.en: Ptarmigan chicks can leave the nest a day after hatching and travel with their parents. They never go back to the nest.
For about a month the chicks can't keep themselves warm, so they snuggle under their mother's belly.
Raichō change feathers three times a year. In winter both males and females turn completely white, hidden against the snow.
In the coldest weather, ptarmigan sometimes dive into the snow to stay out of the wind.
Many alpine plants are a bit poisonous. Chicks eat their mother's droppings soon after hatching to get the special tummy bacteria that help them digest them.
Raichō means "thunder bird". Legend says they come out during thunderstorms and protect against lightning and fire.
Japan's rock ptarmigans are the southernmost rock ptarmigans anywhere on Earth, survivors from the Ice Age.
Japan's government named the raichō an endangered species in 2012 and started a big rescue programme, including protecting chicks in cages at night.

storyVsReal.en: Real raichō chicks stay close to their mother all summer. Hina is a little white chick in winter snow, but real chicks hatch in late June and are brown and mottled for their first months.

text.en: Try balancing on one foot. Wobble? Fall? Count how many times you get back up!
Put a little clay in the bottom of a plastic egg. Push it over. Does it pop back up?
Draw a ptarmigan on white paper in winter colours, and another on brown paper in summer colours. Which hides best?
Play follow-the-leader. In a macaque troop the girls stay together for life!
Find Japan on a map, then the big island of Honshu where the Japanese Alps are.

q.en: Are the animals in Eight Times Up real?

a.en: Yes. Japanese serows, Japanese macaques and rock ptarmigans all live in the Japanese Alps. Each hero file tells you what we changed for the story.
Not quite. It's a goat-antelope, a close cousin of goats, found only in Japan.

q.en: Why are they called snow monkeys?

a.en: Japanese macaques live farther north than any other monkey, in places with deep snow every winter.
Yes, high in the Japanese Alps in summer. Watch quietly, keep your distance and never chase them.
